segments.text: Cats purr because they're happy. Well, that's not exactly true. They also purr when they're scared, hurt, or even giving birth.
The purr starts in the voice box. Tiny muscles there twitch {25|twenty-five} to {150|one hundred fifty} times a second, and the air buzzes on the way in and on the way out.
That's why a cat can purr without stopping to breathe.
Here's the wild part. Kittens can purr when they're just a few days old. They're born blind and deaf, so the purr tells mom: I'm okay.
In fact, some cats have a special feed me purr, with a hidden cry inside it. It sounds a bit like a baby, and humans find it really hard to ignore.
That's not all. Some scientists think those low vibrations might even help bones heal. It's not proven yet, but it's a cool idea.
So cats don't just purr because they're happy. Sometimes a purr means: stay close.
